blocks.html: You already know a great deal of etiquette. You say thank you, you wait your turn, you hold a door. This course takes those habits further: formal dinners, introductions at work, condolence notes, weddings, travel. Before any of that, it helps to know what etiquette is for, because every custom in this course grows from the same root.
Etiquette rests on three ideas: consideration for other people's feelings, respect for every person, and honesty. Its customs exist to put people at ease.

People in a group need ways to get along without stopping to negotiate every small thing. Shared customs do that work. When everyone knows that the host starts the meal or that a reply to an invitation is expected, nobody has to wonder, wait awkwardly, or feel left out. A good custom spares someone a moment of discomfort, and that is the test for any rule you meet: whom does it help, and how?

This is why etiquette is not snobbery. A person who uses the right fork but sneers at someone who used the wrong one has missed the whole point. The sneer causes far more discomfort than the fork ever could. The kindest guests at a formal dinner are often the ones who quietly copy a nervous neighbor's mistake so the neighbor does not feel singled out.

blocks.title: Two guests and a mistake
blocks.q: At a dinner, Kofi drinks from the glass on his left, which belongs to Priya. Nora notices. What should she do?
steps: Ask what would put people at ease. Kofi would be embarrassed by a public correction; Priya needs a glass.
Nora can quietly ask the host for another glass for Priya, or say nothing if Priya has not noticed.
Saying "That's Priya's glass, Kofi" in front of everyone fixes nothing and embarrasses him.
blocks.a: Fix the problem quietly, without drawing attention to Kofi.

blocks.title: Is this rule worth keeping?
blocks.q: A friend says, "Why should I reply to an invitation if I'm not coming? They'll figure it out."
steps: Ask whom the custom helps. The host has to plan food, seats and space.
Without a reply, the host must guess or chase guests, and food may go to waste.
So the custom has a clear reason: replying spares the host work and worry.
blocks.a: Yes: a reply is a small kindness to the host.

blocks.html: Thinking etiquette is a set of snobbish rules for showing off. Every good custom has a reason, usually to spare someone discomfort, and a rule used to embarrass someone defeats its own purpose. Quick check: if following a "rule" would hurt someone's feelings, the kind choice comes first.

Emily Post's Etiquette (1922) is the most famous American etiquette book. Many of its rules, such as calling cards and chaperones, are gone, but its central idea, consideration for others, still holds. This course quotes it only as history.

blocks.html: In Why Etiquette Exists you met the root idea: customs exist to put people at ease. The words manners and etiquette are often used as if they meant the same thing, but it helps to separate them.

Manners are the spirit: kindness, consideration and respect. Etiquette is the specific code a group uses to show that spirit, such as which fork to use or how to address an envelope. Manners stay the same; etiquette changes with time and place.

The spirit and the code solve different problems. Kindness alone does not tell you how a formal dinner runs or how to write to a judge, so a code gives everyone the same expectations. But a code can only point at kindness; it cannot replace it. When the code and the spirit pull apart, as when following a rule would embarrass someone, good manners win.

steps: The code says each fork has its course. The spirit says don't embarrass a guest.
Pointing out her mistake would embarrass her and help no one.
James says nothing and enjoys the meal; the host can bring another fork if needed.
blocks.a: Manners win: let the slip pass quietly.

blocks.html: Treating every etiquette rule as timeless. Many 1922 rules have changed, but the manners behind them, like thanking people and putting guests at ease, have not. Quick check: when a rule seems strange, ask what need it served and whether that need is still met another way.

blocks.html: Since etiquette is a code that changes with time and place, it follows that different families, regions and countries use different codes. This course teaches present-day American custom as its base, with notes where people do things differently. Those notes matter as much as the rules.
Customs vary by region, country and family. As a guest, follow your host's way. Never mock or correct another family's customs: different is not rude, but correcting others is.

The purpose of every custom is to put people at ease. A host's customs are how that home makes people comfortable, so following them honors the host. Telling someone their way is "wrong" does the opposite: it makes them feel judged in their own home or culture. The guest who adapts gracefully is the one practicing good manners.

blocks.html: Calling a different custom "wrong," such as eating with the fork in the left hand or taking shoes off at the door. Different is not rude; correcting others is. Quick check: does this custom cause anyone harm or discomfort? If not, it is simply another way.
Customs differ: when you visit a home or a country with customs you don't know, watch, ask quietly, and follow along. People are almost always glad you asked.

blocks.html: You learned to set the family table: fork on the left, knife and spoon on the right. A restaurant or a dinner party adds more pieces, but the same logic places every one of them. Once you can read that logic, no setting will surprise you.

Bread plate on the left, drinks on the right. Forks go to the left of the plate; knives and spoons to the right, the knife blade facing the plate. You use the utensils from the outside in, one set per course.

A setting is laid out so a guest never has to ask what to use or which glass is theirs. Pieces sit in the order of the meal, so the outermost fork belongs to the first course that needs a fork. The blade faces the plate so no sharp edge points at a neighbor. Bread on the left and drinks on the right keep each guest's things apart from the next person's at a crowded table.

blocks.html: A trick for the crowded table: touch your thumbs to your index fingers and hold the other fingers straight. Your left hand makes a lowercase b (bread) and your right hand a d (drinks). Your bread plate is the one on your left; your glasses are on your right.

blocks.q: At a round table, Sam sees bread plates on both sides of his dinner plate. Which one is his?
steps: Bread goes on the left: make the lowercase b with the left hand.
The plate on his right belongs to the guest on his right.
So he uses the plate on his left, and leaves the other alone even if his neighbor has not touched it.
blocks.a: The one on his left.

Salad is the first course that needs a fork, so it uses the outermost fork.
The fork next to the plate is the dinner fork, for the main course.
blocks.a: The outer fork.

blocks.html: The informal setting already follows the outside-in rule. A formal dinner uses the same rule with more courses, each with its own utensils. Learn the menu order and you can read any formal setting.
Each course has its own utensils, set in the order of use from the outside in. Dessert utensils lie above the plate, and glasses stand above the knives, the water glass first.

A formal setting is a map of the meal. By laying every utensil out ahead of time in the order of the courses, the host spares guests from wondering what comes next, and servers never have to interrupt to hand out forks. The outermost piece always belongs to the next course.

blocks.html: In an informal setting the napkin lies to the left of the forks; at a formal one it rests on the plate. Wherever it starts, it has a small routine of its own.

Place the napkin on your lap after the host does. Blot your mouth rather than wipe it. If you step away during the meal, leave it on your chair or loosely to the left of your plate. At the end, set it loosely to the left of the plate.

Each step keeps the table pleasant for everyone. Waiting for the host lets the host set the pace. Blotting is quiet and tidy. A used napkin stays off the plate and out of sight while you are away, and at the end, a loosely placed napkin tells the host and servers that you are finished without showing anyone a crumpled mess.

blocks.html: Bread and drinks have their own places in the place setting: the bread plate on the left, the glasses on the right. Each has a small custom of its own.

Tear off one bite-size piece of bread at a time and butter it over your bread plate. Take butter from the shared dish onto your bread plate first. Hold a stemmed glass by the stem, and drink only from your own glass, the water glass above your knife.

Breaking one piece at a time keeps crumbs and buttery fingers in one small place, and it lets you talk between bites. Taking butter onto your own plate first keeps your knife and crumbs out of the shared dish, which everyone uses. A glass held by the stem stays cool and clean, and drinking only from your own glass needs no explanation.

blocks.html: You may already hold the fork and knife the American way. Many people, in the U.S. and especially in Europe, use the Continental style instead. Both are correct, and you may meet both at the same table.

American style: cut with the fork in the left hand and the knife in the right, set the knife down on the plate, switch the fork to the right hand, and eat with the tines up. Continental style: keep the fork in the left hand, tines down, and the knife in the right throughout.

Both styles solve the same problem: getting a cut bite to your mouth neatly. American style grew from the habit of eating with the dominant hand; Continental style saves the switch. Neither is ruder. What matters is using one smoothly, because a clumsy mix of the two, waving the knife or stabbing with the fork upright, distracts the people near you.

Customs differ: Continental style is the usual way in much of Europe; American style is common in the U.S. and Canada. Many people switch styles to match the company, and that is fine too.

blocks.html: In either style there comes a moment when you put your utensils down, to talk, to drink, or because you are done. Where you put them sends a silent message to the host and the server.

Resting: utensils stay on the plate, never on the table. In American style the knife rests across the upper right of the plate, blade in, and the fork lies on the plate below it. In Continental style they cross near the tips like an upside-down V, fork over knife, tines down. Finished: fork and knife side by side, diagonally, handles toward 4 o'clock (the lower right), the knife blade facing the fork.

A used utensil laid on the tablecloth leaves food on it and on the table, so once used, it stays on the plate. The resting and finished positions also save words: a server can see from across the room whether to clear your plate, without interrupting you to ask.

blocks.html: A formal setting tells you the order of the courses. Service, the way food is brought and taken away, has its own customs, and so does the moment you begin to eat.
Wait until everyone is served or the host begins; at a large table, start when the host invites you. Food is traditionally served from the left and plates cleared from the right.

Starting together means nobody eats alone while others watch, and the host sets the pace for the whole table. Serving from one side and clearing from the other is a working rule: servers do not collide with each other or reach across a guest's eating hand, and guests learn to lean slightly the other way.

blocks.html: Some foods don't sit still for a fork and knife. With the fork and knife in hand, a few small techniques make them easy.

Spoon soup away from you and sip from the side of the spoon. Twirl long pasta against the plate or a spoon. Eat finger foods with fingers. Remove a pit or bone the way it went in, and set it on the edge of your plate.

Each technique keeps the food on your plate and off your neighbor, your clothes and the cloth. Spooning away from you means any drip falls back in the bowl, not in your lap. Taking a pit out the way it went in, quietly onto a fork or fingertips, means nobody has to watch it happen.

blocks.html: After the courses have been served, a host may raise a glass to welcome guests or honor someone. A toast is a short speech of kindness, and anyone can learn to give one or receive one gracefully.

The host usually gives the first toast. Stand or raise your glass, keep it short and kind, and look at the person being honored. If the toast is to you, stay seated, smile, and don't drink to yourself; then thank everyone and, if you like, toast them back.

A toast gathers the whole table around one kind thought. The host goes first because the host is welcoming everyone. Short is kind: a long speech keeps people holding glasses in the air. The honored person does not drink to themselves for the same reason you don't clap for yourself: the toast is a gift from the others.

blocks.html: A restaurant is a shared dining room. The customs of service you met at a dinner party still apply, plus a few that belong to eating in public.

Reserve if needed and arrive on time. Be courteous to every server and staff member. When someone else is hosting, order at a similar pace and price, and ask what they recommend. Raise problems quietly and kindly.

A reservation lets the restaurant plan tables and staff, and being on time keeps that plan working for every other diner. Courtesy to staff is courtesy to people working hard on your behalf; it also tells your companions a great deal about you. Ordering near your host's price respects their generosity, and a quiet word solves a problem without a scene.

Hey! Over here! We need the check!

blocks.q: James ordered the vegetable curry, and a chicken dish arrives instead. What does he do?
steps: He waits until the server is nearby, rather than calling across the room.
He says quietly, "Excuse me, I think I ordered the vegetable curry."
If his companions are already eating, he tells them to start, and he thanks the server when the right dish comes.

blocks.title: What to order when you are the guest

He orders something in the middle of the range, near what she orders.
He doesn't order the most expensive dish or several extra courses unless she suggests them.
blocks.a: Ask for a recommendation and order near the host's price.

blocks.html: Snapping fingers or waving at servers, or sending food back with a scene. A quiet "Excuse me, when you have a moment" works better. Quick check: would you speak to a friend helping at your own dinner party this way?
Customs differ: in many countries the server will not bring the bill until you ask for it, because rushing a guest is thought rude. Ask for the check when you are ready.

blocks.html: At the end of a restaurant meal comes the bill. Money can make good friends awkward, and a little planning prevents almost all of it.
Traditionally, whoever invites pays. With friends, agree before ordering whether you will split the bill evenly or each pay for what you ordered. Then follow the plan cheerfully.

Clear expectations protect friendships. The person who says "Let me take you to dinner" has offered a gift, so they pay. Among friends, an even split is simple when orders are similar, but unfair when one person ordered much less. Settling it early means nobody orders under a cloud of worry, and nobody argues over a receipt.

blocks.html: After deciding who pays, there is one more line on a U.S. restaurant bill to fill in: the tip. In the U.S., servers at sit-down restaurants earn much of their pay from tips, which is why the custom is so strong here.

At a sit-down restaurant in the U.S., about 15 to 20 percent of the bill before tax is customary, more for great service. Tipping customs differ abroad, where service may be included or tipping not expected.

The tip rewards the work of serving you, and in the U.S. it is a large part of how servers are paid. That is why leaving no tip at a sit-down restaurant, even after slow service, is seen as a slight. Figuring it on the bill before tax makes sense because the tax goes to the government, not to the service. These percentages are a guide, not a law.

blocks.html: You already know how to introduce two people: say the older person's name first and give each a detail to talk about. Adult life adds new settings, such as work, clients and formal events, but the same idea runs through all of them.

Say the honored person's name first, then present the other person to them: an older person, a guest, a client, or a senior colleague. At work, rank decides, not age or gender. Then add a detail so they can start talking.

Saying someone's name first is a small gesture of respect, like holding a door. It tells the honored person, "I am bringing this person to meet you." The added detail does the real work of an introduction: it gives two strangers something to say, so the introducer can step back and the conversation can begin.

steps: At work, rank decides.
James is senior, so his name comes first: "James, I'd like you to meet Ruby Walsh, our new intern. Ruby, this is James Reed, our vice president."

blocks.html: Once you have been introduced, you need to know what to call someone. You learned to use titles with the adults in your life; adults use them with one another, too, especially at first meetings and in writing.
Use a title such as Mr., Ms., Mrs., Mx. or Dr. with the last name until you are invited to use a first name. Always use the name and title a person prefers.

A title is a sign of respect, and starting formal leaves the choice with the other person. Moving from "Ms. Shah" to "Priya" when she invites it is warm; jumping to a first name uninvited can feel presumptuous, especially with older people or at work. Using the name and title a person asks for shows that you listened, which matters more than any rule.

blocks.html: You learned a good handshake as the usual American greeting. And you know that customs differ. Greetings are where the two meet most often.

In the U.S., stand, smile, and shake hands firmly while saying your name. Elsewhere, and with some people here, a bow, a nod, a hand on the heart or a cheek kiss may be usual, and some people prefer not to shake hands at all. Follow the other person's lead.

A greeting says "I see you, and I am glad to meet you." Its form matters less than its warmth. Standing shows respect; a firm, brief handshake is the American way of making that respect physical. When another person offers a different greeting, or none that touches, matching them puts them at ease, which is the whole aim.

He says, "So glad to meet you," and moves on without comment.

Customs differ: a bow is common in Japan and Korea, a cheek kiss among friends in much of Europe and Latin America, and a hand on the heart in many places. Some people avoid handshakes for health, faith or personal reasons. None of these needs comment.

blocks.html: After the greeting comes the conversation. You already know that conversation is a game of catch. Small talk is the warm-up throw: easy topics that let two people find common ground.
Small talk uses safe shared topics, such as the event, travel, books, food or the weather, plus open questions and real listening. It leads to bigger conversations.

Strangers need a little time before they trust each other with anything personal. Small talk gives them that time safely: nobody risks offense by talking about the food or how they know the host. Along the way, people find what they share, a city, a hobby, a favorite book, and a real conversation grows from there. Skipping small talk feels rushed; jumping to personal questions feels intrusive.

"What do you like to do on weekends?"

blocks.q: At a party, Hana asks a stranger, "Do you like this music?" The answer is "Yes." How can she keep the talk going?
steps: A yes-or-no question stops after one word.
An open question invites a story: "What kind of music do you like most?"
Then she listens and asks a follow-up about the answer.
blocks.a: Ask an open question, then follow up on the answer.

blocks.title: A question to skip
blocks.q: Omar meets Kofi at a wedding and is curious about his new job. Which question is better: "How much do they pay you?" or "What do you enjoy most about it?"
steps: Pay is personal and can make someone feel judged or compared.
"What do you enjoy most about it?" invites him to share as much as he likes.

blocks.html: Hosting begins with an invitation. Like small talk, a good invitation is about the other person: it tells guests everything they need so they can say yes with confidence.
A good invitation says who is hosting, what the occasion is, when and where, what to wear if it matters, and how and by when to reply. It also makes clear exactly who is invited.

Every missing detail becomes a question a guest has to ask, or a guess they may get wrong. Without a time, people arrive at different hours; without dress, someone feels out of place; without a reply date, the host cannot plan food. Naming exactly who is invited, on the envelope or in the message, spares everyone the awkward question of whether a partner or children are welcome.

blocks.html: An invitation ends with a request: reply. RSVP comes from the French répondez s'il vous plaît, "please reply." It is one of the clearest rules in etiquette, and one of the most often broken.
Reply by the date asked, in the way asked. "RSVP" asks for a reply either way, yes or no. "Regrets only" asks only those who are not coming to reply.

The host is planning food, chairs and space around your answer. A prompt reply lets them plan; silence leaves them guessing and chasing guests. Once you say yes, the host counts on you, so a reply is a promise: cancel only for a real reason, and as early as you can.

blocks.html: You have replied yes. Now there are two moments that frame every visit: the arrival and the goodbye. Both are about the host's time.
Arrive on time for a dinner, not early; within a reasonable window for a party. Leave before the host looks tired, and thank the host at the door.

A host spends the last minutes before a dinner finishing the food and getting ready, so an early guest catches them unready, while a very late guest can spoil a meal timed to the minute. Parties with an open window are more flexible. At the end, the host will rarely ask anyone to leave, so it falls to guests to notice the signs and say goodnight while everyone is still enjoying themselves.

blocks.html: When you arrive at someone's home for a meal or party, a small gift is a way of saying thank you before the evening even starts.
A small host gift is welcome: flowers already in a vase, a treat, something for the pantry. It is for the host to enjoy later, not to serve that night.

A host has planned the menu and the evening. A gift that must be used right away, such as a dish to serve or loose flowers that need a vase, pulls the host away from guests and into the kitchen, which is the opposite of a thank-you. A gift to enjoy later gives pleasure without adding work.

She brings flowers already arranged in a vase, or a potted plant, or has flowers delivered before or after.

blocks.html: Expecting the host to open and serve what you brought, or bringing cut flowers that pull the host away to find a vase. A host gift says thank you; it should never add work. Customs on host gifts vary by region.

Customs differ: in some regions and families a host gift is expected; in others it is a pleasant extra. In some countries certain flowers or numbers of flowers carry special meanings. Ask someone who knows the custom.

blocks.html: A good guest brings a small gift and arrives on time. A good host has a job, too: to make every guest feel welcome from the moment they arrive.
Greet and introduce guests, ask about food needs ahead, seat the guest of honor at the host's right, keep the talk moving, and put guests at ease.

Guests come for the company more than the food. A host who greets each guest, makes introductions and draws quiet people into the talk gives them what they came for. Asking about allergies and diets ahead spares a guest from going hungry or explaining at the table. The seat at the host's right is a traditional place of honor, so giving it to the guest of honor shows everyone who is being celebrated.

At the table he says nothing to single her out.

blocks.title: A dish that didn't work
blocks.q: Priya's roast is overcooked. Should she apologize to the table?
steps: Apologizing all evening keeps attention on the problem and makes guests feel they must reassure her.

Then she turns the talk to her guests.
blocks.a: Serve it cheerfully and move on.

blocks.html: Spending the party in the kitchen, or apologizing all night for the food. Guests remember a relaxed, welcoming host more than a perfect dish. Choose a menu you can make ahead, so you can be with your guests.

blocks.html: An overnight visit is hosting stretched over days. Host and guest share a home for a while, and small courtesies on both sides keep the visit happy.
A good guest agrees on dates ahead, follows the house routine, keeps their space tidy, offers to help, and sends a thank-you afterward. A good host gives towels, a key and a plan.

Sharing a home means sharing routines: meal times, the bathroom, quiet hours. A clear arrival and departure date lets the host plan work and meals. A guest who fits in with the household, tidies up and helps out lightens the host's load. A host who sets out towels and explains the plan spares the guest from having to ask for every small thing.

blocks.html: You learned the parts of a thank-you note years ago. As an adult you will write them for gifts, dinners, interviews, help in hard times and favors at work. The shape stays the same; the occasions grow.
Write soon. Name the gift or kindness, say how you will use or enjoy it, add a personal line, and close warmly. A handwritten note is still the warmest thanks.

A gift or favor took someone's time, thought or money. A note closes the circle: it tells the giver that the kindness arrived and mattered. Naming the specific gift and how you will use it proves you noticed; a vague "thanks for the gift" could have been written without opening the box. Handwriting takes a few minutes, and the reader can feel that.

Closing and signature: "Warmly, Sam"
blocks.a: A short note that names the dinner and something specific about it.

blocks.title: A late note
blocks.q: Leo got a graduation gift from his uncle two months ago and never wrote. Is it too late?
steps: A late note is always better than no note.
He writes it now, with a light apology: "I'm sorry this is so late."
Then he thanks his uncle as warmly as he would have in June.
blocks.a: No. Write it now.

blocks.html: A condolence note has the same bones as a thank-you note: a greeting, a few sincere lines, a closing. It is harder to write only because the feelings are heavier. Simple words are the right ones.
Say you are sorry for the loss, share a memory or a good quality of the person, offer specific help if you can, and close with sympathy. Keep it short.

A grieving person reads many notes and has little energy. A short note that says "I'm sorry" and shares a memory tells them their loved one mattered to others too, which is a real comfort. Phrases that explain or compare the loss, like "I know how you feel," turn attention away from the grieving person, however kindly meant.

steps: He can't share a memory of her father, so he offers sympathy and a kind thought.

blocks.title: Fixing a line

steps: That line explains the loss, which can feel dismissive to someone grieving.
She replaces it with a memory: "I'll always remember how your mom cheered at every game."
blocks.a: A memory of the person.

blocks.html: Saying nothing for fear of saying the wrong thing, or writing "I know how you feel" or "everything happens for a reason." Simple, sincere words are best, and a short note is far better than none. Quick check: is every line about them and the person they lost?
Customs differ: families of different faiths and traditions mourn in different ways. A note of sympathy is welcome in nearly all of them; follow the family's lead about visits and gifts.

blocks.html: A thank-you note is a short letter. Longer letters, to a landlord, a school, a company or a grandparent, use the same frame with a body in the middle.
A letter has the date, a greeting ("Dear Ms. Grant,"), the body in short paragraphs, a closing ("Sincerely," or "Warmly,") and your signature. Match the closing to how well you know the reader.

The frame tells the reader at a glance when the letter was written, who it is for and who sent it, which matters when letters are filed or answered weeks later. Short paragraphs, one idea each, make the request easy to find. The closing sets the tone: "Sincerely" is respectful for anyone; "Love" belongs to family and close friends.

The reader can now find the question at once.

blocks.html: A letter needs an envelope the post office can read. Addressing it well uses what you learned about titles and names, plus a layout every U.S. mail carrier expects.
The recipient's name and address go in the center, your return address in the upper left, and the stamp in the upper right. Use titles and full names, and include the ZIP code.

Mail is sorted by machines and people who read the center block first, so the delivery address belongs there, with the ZIP code on the last line. The return address in the corner lets an undeliverable letter come back to you. The stamp goes in the upper right, where the canceling machines expect it. A title and full name are a courtesy to the reader, and they help the letter reach the right person in a shared home.

blocks.html: Email follows the same frame as a letter: a greeting, a body, a closing and your name. What changes is speed, which makes it easy to send something you will wish you had read again.
Write a clear subject, open with a greeting, keep it brief, proofread, and reply within a day or two. Use "reply all" only when everyone needs the reply.

A subject line lets busy people find your message and know what it is about before they open it. A greeting and a closing keep the tone friendly in a medium where tone is easy to misread. Short messages respect the reader's time. Email is permanent and easy to forward, so writing as if the whole office might read it is simply prudent. "Reply all" fills many inboxes at once, so it is for replies everyone truly needs.

steps: Forty people do not need to read his thanks.
If he wants to thank the manager, he replies only to her, or says nothing at all.
blocks.a: No. Reply only to the sender, if at all.

blocks.html: You learned that the people in front of you come first. As an adult you carry the phone into meals, meetings, performances, trains and waiting rooms. The rule is the same; the places multiply.
Silence the phone at meals, meetings and performances. Step away to take a call. Keep speakerphone, videos and music off in shared spaces unless you use headphones.

A ringing phone or a glance at a screen tells the person in front of you that someone else might matter more. In shared spaces such as a bus, a waiting room or a theater, your sound becomes everyone's sound, and they cannot step away from it. Silencing the phone and stepping aside for calls keeps your conversations from becoming other people's burden.

blocks.html: You know the basics of texting courtesy: reasonable hours, clear words, a read before you send. With phones in company handled, adult texting adds one more question: is a text the right way to say this at all?
Mind the hour, the tone and the length. Don't send important or sad news by text when a call or visit is possible. Answer within a reasonable time.

A text arrives without your voice or face, so the reader must guess your tone, and short texts often read colder than they were meant. That is fine for "running 5 minutes late," but serious news, such as a breakup, a resignation or a death, deserves the comfort of a voice. Texts also arrive whenever you send them, so a 2 a.m. message can wake someone; late texts can wait for morning.

blocks.html: Social media is messaging with an audience. A post can reach hundreds of people, including some you never meant it for, and it can last for years.
Ask before posting photos of others or their children. Don't announce other people's news. Remember that posts are public and lasting.

A photo or a piece of news belongs, in part, to the people in it. A friend may not want a photo seen by an employer, or may want to tell family about an engagement or a pregnancy in their own words before the world knows. Asking first gives them that choice. And because posts can be copied and found later, writing only what you would be glad to see quoted keeps both you and others safe from embarrassment.

blocks.html: You learned the basics of video calls and of phones in company. A video meeting for work or school joins the two: it is a room you walk into, even if it is on a screen.
Join on time, check your sound and background, mute when you are not speaking, look at the camera, and give the meeting your attention.

Everyone in a video meeting has blocked out the same minutes. Joining late or fumbling with sound wastes everyone's time at once. Background noise from an open microphone drowns out whoever is speaking, which is why muting matters. Looking at the camera is how you make eye contact on a screen, and keeping your attention on the meeting is the same courtesy you would show in a room.

blocks.html: A job interview puts many skills from this course to work at once: small talk, greetings, listening and a thank-you note. For the practical side of finding and applying for a job, see Apply for a Job in Being an Adult.
Arrive a few minutes early, dress a step above the job's usual dress, greet everyone kindly, listen, ask good questions, and send a thank-you within a day.

An interview is a short glimpse of what working with you would be like. Being early shows that you respect the interviewer's schedule. Dressing a step up shows you took the meeting seriously. Kindness to everyone, from the front desk to the interviewer, shows how you treat people when you are not trying to impress them, and a prompt thank-you shows follow-through.

blocks.html: After an interview, you will meet dress codes at work and at weddings, parties and dinners. The words can sound like a secret language, but each one names a step on a ladder from most to least formal.
Social dress codes run from white tie and black tie to cocktail, smart casual and casual. At work they run from business formal to business casual and casual. When unsure, ask the host.

A dress code helps guests feel comfortable, because no one wants to be the only person in jeans at a black-tie dinner, or the only one in a tuxedo at a picnic. Dressing for the occasion is also a way of showing respect for the host, who has planned an event of a certain kind. Since the terms are not always clear, asking is always polite.

blocks.html: Meetings are where colleagues share time, the way guests share a table. The courtesies of an interview, being on time, listening and following through, carry straight into them.
Be on time, come prepared, let others finish, keep to the topic, credit others' ideas, and follow up on what you promised.

A meeting costs every person in the room the same hour, so lateness and wandering talk waste many hours at once. Letting people finish lets the best ideas come out, not just the loudest. Crediting a colleague's idea is both honest and generous: it builds the kind of trust that makes people share ideas with you. Following up shows that your word means something.

blocks.html: After meetings, the office kitchen, the break room, the copier and the shared fridge are where colleagues meet most often. These spaces belong to everyone, which means everyone takes care of them.
Clean up after yourself, label and clear out your food, don't take what isn't yours, keep calls and smells modest, and refill what you empty.

In a shared space, every small mess becomes someone else's job. A dish left "to soak" is a dish a colleague has to move; an empty coffee pot greets the next tired person. Labels and weekly clean-outs keep the fridge from turning into a mystery. Strong smells and loud calls reach everyone nearby. The rule is easy: leave it as you would want to find it.

blocks.html: A wedding invitation calls on everything you know about replying, dress codes and gifts. It is a day the couple has planned for a long time, and a good guest helps it go the way they hoped.
Reply on time, bring only the guests named on the invitation, follow the dress code, give a gift (often from the registry), and let the couple shine.

A wedding is planned to the seat: caterers need a count, and every added guest costs money and space. That is why the reply date matters and why only those named are invited. The registry tells guests what the couple would like, which spares everyone guesswork. And the day is about the couple, so a guest's job is to celebrate them, not to draw attention.

blocks.html: A condolence note is one way to show sympathy. Going to a funeral or memorial is another, and it often matters even more to the family.
Dress in quiet colors, arrive early, sign the guest book, follow the family's customs, and offer the family short, sincere words: "I'm so sorry. She was a wonderful teacher."

Families remember who came. Being there says "your loss matters to us" more clearly than words. Quiet dress and an early arrival keep the focus where it belongs and avoid disturbing the service. The guest book tells the family later who came. Services differ by faith and family, so following their lead respects their way of mourning.

blocks.html: After the funeral, the grieving family returns to everyday life, often when the visits and cards have stopped. This is when friends can help most.
Keep visits short, listen more than you talk, offer specific help ("I'll bring dinner Tuesday"), and keep in touch in the weeks after.

Grief is tiring, and a grieving person may not have the energy to host. A short visit gives comfort without demanding much. Listening lets them talk about the person they lost, which many people want to do. A specific offer is easier to accept than "let me know if you need anything," which leaves the work of asking to them. And the weeks after the funeral are often the loneliest, so a call or a card then means a great deal.

She listens, and if Mrs. Hale wants to share stories about Walt, she listens to those, too.
Before leaving, she makes a specific offer: "I'll mow your lawn on Saturday."
blocks.a: Short, mostly listening, with a specific offer.

steps: No. Many cards and visits stop after the funeral.

blocks.a: Not at all: reach out now.

blocks.html: Visiting someone in the hospital, or a family with a new baby, uses the same care as visiting the bereaved: short visits and specific help. The person you are visiting needs rest more than company.
Ask before visiting, keep it short, stay home if you are sick, wash your hands, and offer help with meals or errands rather than asking to hold the baby.

Patients and new parents are tired, and their days are full of care, feedings and doctors' visits. Asking first lets them choose a good time, or say not yet. A short visit gives cheer without draining them. Staying home when you are sick and washing your hands are widely agreed ways to protect someone recovering or a newborn. Help with meals or errands lightens their load in a way a visit alone cannot.

blocks.html: Gifts run through every occasion in this unit, from weddings to new babies. A good gift is about the person who receives it, and so is a good thank-you.
Choose with the person in mind, include a gift receipt when it may help, and thank every gift. Regifting is debated; most agree it must be new and never go back to the same circle.

A gift says "I thought about you." Choosing with the person's tastes in mind, and not your own, is what makes it feel personal. A gift receipt lets them exchange it without awkwardness. Thanking every gift, even one you don't love, honors the thought behind it. Regifting divides opinion because it can hurt the original giver if it is discovered; that is why those who accept it insist on care and discretion.

blocks.html: Borrowing and lending are everyday consideration in action. A borrowed ladder or car carries the lender's trust along with it.
Ask before you borrow. Return the item on time, in as good shape or better. Replace what you break or use up. Lend only what you can afford to lose.

A lender does you a favor and takes a small risk. Returning the item on time means they don't have to chase you, and returning it in good shape, cleaned, refilled or with a full tank, turns a favor into a pleasure. Replacing what you break shows that you value their trust above the cost. And lending only what you could do without keeps a broken dish from becoming a broken friendship.

blocks.html: Neighbors are people you borrow and lend with, wave to every morning and share walls, fences and streets with. Small courtesies make years of living side by side pleasant.
Greet neighbors. Keep noise, pets and yard tidy. Park considerately. Warn them about a party or a big project. Talk to them directly, and kindly, about a problem.

Your home is next to theirs, so your sounds, pets, cars and yard become part of their home too. A friendly hello builds goodwill for the day you need a favor or have to raise a concern. A heads-up about a party or a roofing job lets them plan. When something bothers you, a direct, friendly word gives them a chance to fix it, while going to a landlord or posting online first turns a small issue into a feud.

blocks.html: Travel puts you shoulder to shoulder with strangers, like the neighbors you will only have for one flight. The same courtesy works: think about the people around you.
On planes and trains, store bags quickly, recline gently, share the armrest (the middle seat gets both), keep calls short and quiet, and thank the crew and hotel staff.

In a narrow aisle, one slow traveler holds up everyone behind. A seat slammed back can spill a drink or hit a knee, so a glance back and a gentle recline spare the person behind you. The middle seat has the least room, so many travelers let that passenger have both armrests. Crews and hotel staff serve many tired travelers, and a thank-you makes their day better.

blocks.html: Travel courtesy gets you there; respect for local ways makes you a welcome guest once you arrive. It is when customs differ on the scale of a whole country.

Before traveling, learn a greeting and "thank you" in the local language, how people dress for sacred and formal sites, and the local customs on tipping, greetings and shoes. Ask, watch and follow local ways.

When you visit another country, you are a guest in it. A few words in the local language say "I took the trouble to meet you halfway," and people almost always respond warmly. Dress customs at sacred places and the local habits on tipping or greetings are how that country puts people at ease. Assuming home customs apply everywhere can embarrass both you and your hosts.

blocks.html: Everyone forgets a name sometimes, often right after an introduction. What matters is how gracefully you handle it, and how kindly you help others when they forget yours.
Admit it lightly ("I'm so sorry, your name has slipped my mind"), or introduce yourself first so the other person offers theirs. When someone forgets your name, say it for them.

A forgotten name is a tiny slip that everyone understands. Trying to hide it, by avoiding the person or skipping an introduction, makes the moment far more awkward and can leave someone out. A light admission takes two seconds, and offering your own name first gives the other person an easy chance to say theirs. Helping someone who has forgotten your name spares them the same discomfort.

Or she admits it lightly: "I'm so sorry, your name has slipped my mind."
She does not skip the introduction and leave Leo standing.

blocks.html: Accidents happen at every table: a knocked glass, a dropped plate, a stain on a host's rug. Like any small slip in etiquette, the goal is to put everyone back at ease quickly.
Apologize briefly, help clean up, offer to pay for any damage, and move on. As a host, reassure the guest and make light of it.

After a spill, everyone feels a moment of tension, and the guest who caused it feels worst. One sincere apology and quick help fix the mess and settle the moment. Apologizing again and again keeps everyone's attention on the accident and forces others to keep reassuring. A host who laughs it off tells the guest that they matter more than the rug.

blocks.a: Reassure the guest and make light of it.

blocks.html: After your own spills and slips, the harder question: what about someone else's? A friend with spinach in her teeth, a guest using the wrong fork, a coworker who mispronounces a word.
Tell someone privately about something they would want to fix, like spinach in their teeth or an open zipper. Never correct another person's table manners or grammar in front of others.

Some slips the person would want to know about, because they can fix them in a second and would be embarrassed to find out later; a quiet word is a kindness. Other slips, like the wrong fork or a grammar mistake, harm no one, and pointing them out in front of others only causes embarrassment. Correcting others publicly is a bigger breach than almost any mistake it points out.

steps: He can fix it in a second and would hate to give a toast with it.
She leans in and says quietly, "You have a little something in your teeth," or touches her own tooth as a signal.
blocks.a: Tell him quietly, right away.

steps: It harms no one.

blocks.a: Say nothing.

blocks.html: Sometimes the rude one is someone else. You learned to handle other people's slips kindly; a rude remark or a nosy question calls for the same calm.
Stay calm. Ask "Why do you ask?", give a short neutral answer, change the subject, or simply say, "I'd rather not discuss that." You never owe a personal answer.

Answering rudeness with rudeness makes two rude people instead of one, and it often feeds the argument. A calm reply keeps your dignity and usually ends the moment. A nosy question, about money, weight, age, or why you are not married or have no children, is not owed an answer: a polite deflection protects your privacy without starting a fight.

steps: She doesn't owe a personal answer.

blocks.a: A light, short answer and a change of subject.

steps: He stays calm and doesn't trade insults.
"Maybe! Simple ideas are sometimes the ones that work. What would you change?"
Inviting a better idea turns the remark back into a discussion.
blocks.a: Stay calm and invite the other person's idea.

blocks.html: Like answering a rude remark, declining takes calm and kindness. Invitations, second helpings, favors and requests all sometimes need a no.
Decline invitations, food and requests kindly and briefly: "Thank you for asking; I can't make it." A long excuse isn't needed, and a lie isn't either.

A kind, clear no respects the other person: they can plan, ask someone else or move on. A long excuse invites argument or questions, and an invented one can be found out, which hurts more than the no would have. Saying yes and then not showing up is the worst choice of all, because the other person counted on you. Thanks, a clear answer and warmth are all a no needs.

blocks.html: Asking someone on a date uses the same courtesy as any invitation, and answering uses what you learned about declining kindly. Clear, kind words on both sides make it easy for everyone.
Ask clearly, in person or by a call when you can, and make the plan specific. Accept a "no" gracefully. When you are the one asked, answer kindly and truthfully either way.

A clear, specific invitation ("Would you like to get coffee on Saturday afternoon?") is easy to answer; a vague one ("We should hang out sometime") leaves the other person guessing what you mean. Accepting a no gracefully respects the other person's choice and keeps a friendship or a workplace comfortable. A truthful answer, yes or no, is kinder than a "maybe" that keeps someone waiting.

steps: He accepts it the first time: "No problem, thanks for letting me know."
He does not ask why or ask again later in the week.
He stays friendly as before.
blocks.a: Accept it gracefully and stay friendly.

blocks.html: Once a plan is made and accepted, a date is a chance to get to know someone. The courtesies are the ones you already know from restaurants, phones and conversation. One question, who pays, comes back from splitting the bill.
Be on time, put the phone away, listen, and be kind to staff. Settle who pays ahead: customs range from the inviter paying to splitting, and both are polite.

Being on time and putting the phone away say "you matter to me tonight." Listening is how two people get to know each other. Kindness to servers and staff shows how a person treats everyone, which is worth knowing. Who pays is a matter where writers disagree, so the courteous thing is to settle it early and without pressure, so the meal can be about the company.

steps: By the old custom, the one who invited pays, and Ruby can simply take the check.

Better still: settle it when making the plan.

blocks.html: You learned to stand to greet people. Posture and presence are that same courtesy carried through a whole conversation: the way you stand, sit and pay attention tells people they matter.
Stand tall and relaxed, sit upright, rise to greet, look people in the face, and keep your hands still. Presence means giving people your full attention.

Posture here is a matter of poise and courtesy. Standing tall and easy, without stiffness, and facing the person you are talking with shows that you are glad to be there. Sitting upright at the table, with feet on the floor, keeps you part of the conversation. Still hands and a face turned toward the speaker say "I am listening." People remember how attentive you were far longer than how you looked.

blocks.name: et-posture
blocks.cap: Drag from slumped to poised. Poise is tall and easy, not stiff.

steps: He moves the drink to his left hand, so his right is free and dry for a handshake.
He stands tall, faces her, smiles and says his name.
He listens, looking at her face rather than around the room.
blocks.a: Free the right hand, face her, and give her his attention.

steps: Sitting upright, feet on the floor.
Turning toward the speaker and listening, with a nod or a question at the end.

Customs differ: in some cultures, steady eye contact with an elder or a superior can seem forward, and a slightly lowered gaze shows respect. Follow the other person's lead.
